notes.title: How the cuisine filters were policed
notes.body: Every food card names a specific dish — a cuisine label alone doesn’t qualify. Discovery started from what Philadelphia is famous for: the cheesesteak (measured — the famous Pat’s/Geno’s rivalry versus the locals’ and critics’ picks), the roast pork Italian, the hoagie, tomato pie, soft pretzels, water ice, scrapple and Tastykake; then Reading Terminal Market, the Italian Market, the Mexican kitchens of South 9th Street, the Vietnamese and Cambodian kitchens of Washington Ave and South Philly, and the Michelin and James Beard bench. A cuisine tag names the kitchen’s own tradition, never one dish it happens to serve; gaps are stated, not padded.

places.w: Corner-storefront pasta and wine bar from Waywine Vineyards' crew — LaBan's 'Fishtown hit' review praises the ruffled mafalde and beet-pink ravioli with Pennsylvania wines; on the Infatuation's 15 best in Fishtown.

Marcie Turney and Valerie Safran's Mediterranean small-plates bar (2010) that turned 13th Street into Midtown Village's dining strip — Philly Mag Best of Philly (Best Dessert), Inquirer, Visit Philly.

Turney and Safran's cosy Italian-American spot with a garden courtyard — Philly Mag Best of Philly (Best Outdoor Dining) and best-meatballs pick, Infatuation review, Thrillist's best Italian restaurants in the US (PhillyVoice), Visit Philly.

Iron Chef Masaharu Morimoto's first American restaurant, opened with Stephen Starr in 2001 — set the local standard for modern Japanese dining and helped put Philly on the national map; Philly Mag Best of Philly (Best Japanese), Inquirer, Infatuation, Visit Philly.

Joey Baldino's 35-seat Sicilian BYOB (2011) — the Vetri/Osteria alum's tribute to Anna Tasca Lanza's Sicily; LaBan 'passion in every dish' review, one of the region's best $55 prix fixes per the Inquirer's Collingswood guide, Philly Mag, 6abc.
